In recent experiments, we found that GLM 5.3 can autonomously compromise recent versions of Mozilla Firefox using security fixes that have been published but not yet shipped to users.

We used a deliberately basic setup meant to emulate a relatively unsophisticated attacker with limited resources. After basic initial instructions to inspect those not-yet-shipped fixes, the model reliably built successful exploits for six recent Firefox versions on its own using only information available at the time of release.

These exploits, which cost about $1,000 per compromised version, would let an attacker steal passwords and authentication cookies stored in the browser, or read any files on the user's computer, after the user opens a single webpage, with no further interaction.

The exploits make use of the "patch gap," the time between when security fixes are made public in beta or "nightly" software updates and when those fixes are generally released to users. Until now, exploiting it required significant human time and skill, or special access to frontier models with advanced cyber capabilities.

Our results show that widely available open-weight models can now do this relatively cheaply and quickly. We gave GLM 5.3 up to 48 hours to find an exploit, but its fastest attempt needed only 12 hours.

In all of its successful attacks, the patch gap gave GLM 5.3 an initial foothold in the browser. To turn that foothold into reading files off the user's computer, the model also independently discovered and used a previously unpublished vulnerability.

We shared our findings with Mozilla, which patched the vulnerability in its October 27 Firefox 159.0 release. We haven't yet confirmed whether the attack still succeeds without it, but expect the fix makes it substantially harder. We're grateful to Mozilla for their responsiveness and collaboration.

Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.

Meantime, the ECI shows a sharp rise in health insurance costs pushing up U.S. employers’ benefit costs, even as growth in wages and salaries slows.

Wage growth has slowed to 3.1% as of Q3, while benefit costs are up 3.9%. Benefit cost growth has traditionally run slightly below wages, but now it is running slightly above them.

This means workers are getting less of their compensation as pay and more in insurance premiums, which are driven mostly by things outside of employers' control.

This raises a few questions: Do higher fixed costs for workers on health coverage lead businesses to hire more cautiously (or shift to part-time workers who don't get benefits)? And note: if employers respond by passing more costs onto workers through higher premiums or less coverage, the ECI won't capture this.

Every year, over half a million women develop cervical cancer, and more than 300,000 die from the disease. These deaths are particularly tragic because we can prevent them through vaccination and early screening.

Because cervical cancer is caused by a virus — the “human papillomavirus” (HPV) — it can be prevented through vaccination. HPV vaccines are highly effective, as demonstrated in large-scale randomized controlled trials. Research shows that, if given early, vaccination reduces the risk of serious cervical cell changes by 99% for the HPV types most likely to cause cervical cancer.

In England, younger cohorts vaccinated at school show dramatically lower rates of cervical cancer than older cohorts when they reach the same age. In the youngest cohort, which had a vaccination rate of 89%, cervical cancer rates were around 87% lower than in the oldest cohort.

Yet HPV vaccination rates are low, or vaccines are unavailable in many countries. In many countries across Africa and Asia, HPV vaccines are not offered routinely at no cost at a national level.

Higher vaccination rates could prevent hundreds of thousands of cervical cancer cases every year. Researchers Kate T. Simms and colleagues estimate that 80% to 100% vaccination rates for both boys and girls, with catch-up vaccinations for adults, could prevent nearly 50 million cervical cancer cases by 2100.

By investing in vaccination and screening, the world could save hundreds of thousands of lives each year, prevent avoidable suffering, and make cervical cancer a disease of the past.

At @MarketUrbanism , @salimfurth comments on the disappointing fade of the English New Homes Bonus program.

I had never heard of this program until I was working on something else, asked Claude to recommend me some literature, and it recommended me something on the NHB program... and then I was flabbergasted I'd never heard of it.

The NHB at its peak provided English localities with SIX YEARS of property-tax-revenue-equivalents for every new home they permitted. This was thousands of pounds of direct revenue for every home. They spent billions of pounds on this program from 2011-2026 (it has just this year been eliminated).

So, did paying English localities to permit housing work?

Well, I had Claude figure it out. The answer is... maybe slightly?

I instructed Claude to study 4 different ways of analyzing if the program boosted homebuilding. 

First, leveraging a rule change in 2017 that excluded a bunch of localities, we can see if losing the NHB reduced permitting. Answer: no, in fact they maybe increased their permitting after losing the NHB. However, this isn't a clean test: they may have increased their permitting in order to get back into the NHB program by getting over the 0.4% stock additional threshold. So this one is a "Maybe the program kinda worked?" answer.

Second, I was curious about a learning mechanism. You can imagine that pre-NHB, localities that had a "big year" of permitting may have then had "big years" of paperwork, disruptions, and costs, and so "big years" would cause subsequent reductions in permitting. But post-NHB, you can imagine that "big years" of permitting would cause big windfalls of revenues, so might nudge localities to "learn" to permit more. Did Claude find evidence for this? No, not at all. In fact "big years" for permitting seem associated with more NEGATIVE post-year permitting in the post-NHB than the pre-NHB period. Yikes. Talking with @salimfurth he noted that in the post-2017 era, localities might have incentivizes to cluster their permitting all in one year to get over the 0.4% threshold, which could bias these results. Fair.

Third, the NHB was a WAY bigger budgetary impact for some localities (Shire districts) than for others, just because the ratio of new housing construction to municipal budgets varies widely. You'd expect the "more exposed" districts to increase permitting more. The effect here at first seems promising: Shire districts DID have big increases in permits granted! But this is because they had big increases in permits applied for; the actual *rate of granting a permit* DECLINES for Shire districts, despite the NHB literally *paying them to approve*. Moreover, the rise in approvals clearly has a pre-trend before NHB rolled out. NHB also paid localities to clear out long-term empty homes, but we see no Shire-specific reduction in long-term empty homes. So this all suggests little to no effect.

Fourth and finally, the NHB applied *in England only*. We can look at England vs. Wales and Scotland, and then specifically at *municipalities near the borders of England* to see if they changed in a unique way. The answer here is.... maybe? It does look like both the whole regions AND the border-regions only did have higher permitting in England, but it is VERY modest and noisy.

On the whole, this seems like a very big, expensive experiment telling us that "pay for permitting" may not work very well at all. cc @aarmlovi @SCP_Hughes @PeterRFB @johnarnold 

As an aside, this is, I think, a fun case of what Claude allows for researchers. Claude caused my awareness of this program which gets shockingly little attention. I didn't have time to do tons of elaborate analyses myself, so I literally just came up with four possible tests of how the program could be evaluated, and told Claude "here are four ways you could test the program to see if it worked; go do these tests and make sure you use best research practices and very good methods along the way"

Claude didn't do perfectly, and I hope a human housing scholar will go investigate in more detail. But being able to run basically four different quasi-causal models on an intervention *the same afternoon I learned of its existence* and doing so at <1 hour time cost to me, the researcher... y'all, AI is the real deal.

We wouldn’t be surprised to see GPU rental revenue reach $100bn per gigawatt a year.

Nebius ($NBIS) has already reported a short-term deal in the $40m–$50m per MW annualised range. That is $40bn–$50bn per GW. Likewise for Space $SPCX and others while $CRWV sold its long term capacity too early at low prices. 

Use 660,000 Blackwell GPUs as a simplified 1GW case. With every GPU-hour rented:
• $50bn a year = $8.65 per GPU-hour.
• $100bn a year = $17.30 per GPU-hour.

DeepSeek reports $38 of API revenue per GPU-hour at off-peak prices for a V4.1 Flash cluster. Peak tariffs are double. Serving the same workload at those prices would imply $76 per GPU-hour.

For an inference provider that can reproduce those economics on rented hardware, a move from $5–$6 rent to $9 can still be affordable. Even roughly $18 need not make the service uneconomic.

Suppose another provider achieves 70% of that $38–$76 revenue benchmark across its rented GPU-hours. That gives $26.60–$53.20 of revenue per hour. After $18 of GPU rent, $8.60–$35.20 remains for other costs and profit.

The condition is matching DeepSeek’s serving efficiency on the rented hardware and sustaining paid demand at those token prices. Releasing the inference code does not guarantee either.

For operators that can do this, we think there is room to keep bidding up scarce GPU capacity, even at twice today’s roughly $9 hourly rate.

卧槽！缠论里最复杂的分型、笔、中枢识别，居然有人全部用 Rust 重写了，还整合了 220 多个交易信号函数！

CZSC，6.5K Stars，一套专门做缠论分析和量化策略研究的 Python 工具。

以前研究缠论，最麻烦的就是手动画笔、找中枢、判断买卖点，不同周期还得反复对照。

这套框架直接把缠论结构识别、信号组合、策略回测串起来，最新 1.0 版本还将核心算法迁移到了 Rust。

核心能力：

1️⃣ 自动识别缠论：分型、笔、中枢自动计算，不用手动在 K 线上画

2️⃣ 220+ 交易信号：内置大量信号函数，可以组合不同条件研究买卖机会

3️⃣ 多周期分析：同时处理 1 分钟、5 分钟、30 分钟、日线等 K 线数据

4️⃣ 策略回测：将信号转成交易规则，支持历史回放、持仓权重回测和收益分析

5️⃣ 行情数据接入：支持 Tushare、天勤、CCXT，覆盖 A 股、期货和 Crypto

6️⃣ K 线可视化：基于 Plotly 和 Lightweight Charts，自动展示缠论结构和交易信号

更有意思的是，它不只是一个画缠论线条的指标。

比如研究 A 股 30 分钟走势，可以先自动识别分型、笔和中枢，再结合日线信号筛选机会，最后拿历史数据回测。

而且 Python 可以直接调用 Rust 核心算法，不用自己从零实现整套缠论逻辑。

做 A 股量化、缠论研究或者 Crypto 策略开发的，这套确实值得收藏！

对某些小团体、以及某“男明星”的声讨

首先，还是先表明成分。咱第一次接触邦多利是在大概7-8年前，大概在邦一播出一年后看的（咱当时还在玩阴阳师、荒野行动呢）。不过当时也没有什么大少女乐队时代，除了邦一就是轻音，所以后续也没太多了解。后来，在24年末，咱又通过音游的方式再次接触并入坑了邦多利。所以，咱说是老资历也算不上，但也不是什么小资历了

开门见山地讲，小团体的头头，那些确实跑了不少线下的人，我敢肯定，绝大多数是日留，或者是其他长期居住在日本的人（当然有很多邦友会经常飞日本看live，但某些群体已经超出这个范围，把发售会等其他线下活动也算入其中了）。说真的，身处在日本，有更多机会跑线下不是很正常的事啊，并不能成为炫耀的资本（就像咱不会炫耀咱在英国收集绝版战锤模型很方便一样）如果对那些群体而言，更方便跑线下以便炫耀才是他们选择长期留在日本的主要原因的话，未免有些过于可悲了吧…如果你们追求高人一等的感觉，又何必留在邦多利这个圈子内呢，向更好更优越的地方行进不好吗———还是说，你们的能力仅限于此了呢？如果真是这样，没有能力又妄求优越感的你们更显得可笑而可悲了…

然后是那些小团体的小弟。揭开遮羞布，无非是一群只跑过几次线下，又想寻求优越感，于是认大哥，在大哥无理取闹的时候为他们冲锋的人了。实话说，你们比你们的大哥更可笑。你们的大哥至少还有能力留在日本天天跑线下，你们连做到这个的能力、条件都没有，却又想高人一等———是想打肿脸充胖子吗？（很像是在正常live场中买个最便宜的d票在最后排模仿无限制场起飞、甩手、光害，影响他人的群体呢）

这些小团体最看不起的群体，却以自己的方式，为邦多利创造更高的价值呢。事实上，优质的二创，如画图、写文，以及做mad和其他二创视频被正主翻牌看见、转帖，甚至能上邦TV或者直播———这些互动不比小团体的那些人仅仅在线下转瞬即逝的互动好多了吗？所以，小团体最看不上的，才是他们最嫉妒，最渴望的呢

话题转回最近很嚣张的某个男明星。最初咱以为某人只是上头的粉丝，没想到原来不仅是认知厨，还是个下头的，天天意淫的男友粉啊。某人的动态、评论中，字里行间中都流露着对女性的蔑视（咱虽然是男生，但咱也是平权主义者啊。咱讨厌极端女权，咱也讨厌某些大男子主义者啊），说真的，某人干脆改姓禅院算了，禅院依火这名字也不错，挺适合某人的言论的。就凭某人恶劣的品行，别说追到喜欢的推了，只要是正常的女生，都不会喜欢一个如此恶劣的男性———你有什么脸面觉得对方会喜欢你一个下头男啊。况且，某人的言论不是很专一呢，绝对是那种谈几天就会出轨的类型吧。况且，仅凭单方面的言论，就意淫对方倒贴自己的人，如此厚颜无耻之人，咱还是第一次见———自己几斤几两不清楚吗？最后，还是恭喜你如愿以偿地出名了，你和你的小团体现在在全世界的邦多利爱好者中都已经恶名昭彰了呢

最后的最后，守护最好的阿拉蕾，守护最好的yuno，守护最好的梦限大，守护最好的邦多利

After listening to the FDA’s full presentation of the new @FDA guidelines for individualized genome editing products I can’t emphasise enough just how much of a game-changer they really are - for Gene Editing-based treatments such as Prime Editing $PRME and Base Editing $BEAM!

IMO the key difference between the current regulatory framework for approving new genetic treatments and the FDA’s new proposed guidelines is that different variants of the same gene will no longer be considered by the FDA as a new clinical indication - which requires a new clinical trail, but instead all that it would require from Beam or Prime in order to receive a regulatory approval would be to submit a BLA supplement which is huge! 

As of now these new FDA guidelines will be relevant only for individualized Gene Editing products meaning therapies that use Gene Editing technology to correct specific, patient-unique disease-causing genetic variants and which intended to prevent, treat, or cure a monogenic disease or condition caused by known pathogenic gene variants, where all product variants in the BLA are designed to achieve the same editing outcome.

This is absolutely tremendous and super exciting for the entire Gene Editing field!

Semiconductor chokepoints are huge strategic assets: Taiwan is building its Silicon Shield, Korea is near-untouchable due to HBM, America is building AGI with Nvidia chips.

Yet despite ASML, Europe captures little AI value and even less strategic leverage. Why?

(1) No BATNA. If ASML stops exporting to Taiwan, it loses all its revenue, if it starts exporting to China, America starts cutting off essential components. And it sells no machines to Europe at all--so whenever anyone starts thinking about 'using' the ASML chokepoint, everyone else calls the bluff.

(2) No political awareness. European governments are trapped in dogmatic slumber, unwilling and unable to treat ASML as a strategic asset. As a result, Washington feels like it has to run European export policy instead. Every other country uses its bottlenecks, but Europe pretends it can’t.

(3) No inspiration. There's no project, no vehicle, nothing to actively choose. Weaponising export controls just to annoy great powers isn't very motivating; policymakers ask 'what for?'. Right now, there's no good answer.

That means there's a gap in Europe's AI strategy: an ambitious play, a conduit for political attention, and an alternative use for ASML machines all at once.

The timing is right: all this is happening just as the chip industry is about to be upended and accelerated by AI systems that uplift chip and process design. In the next years, we might close the hardware loop for recursive self-improvement: use models to build better chips which we use to train even better models to build even better chips.

For that loop, chip fabrication is one central bottleneck.

That's why I believe the gap in Europe's strategy is fab-shaped. I suspect the best way to fill it is to enlist and subsidise ASML and imec and to recruit TSMC and American frontier labs to build a leading R&D chip facility in Europe: Eurofab.

2027年6月期1Q経常利益は147億円。市場予想263億円を約44%下回る厳しい内容。

ただし、今回の未達をAI半導体需要の減速と直結させるのは早計では？

■ 決算内容を詳しく見ると
　※生産は伸びている

・半導体関連装置売上：前年比▲42.9%
・同装置の生産実績：＋120.2%
・サービス売上：＋31.2%
・前受金：前期末比約428億円増加
・仕掛品：約156億円増加
・売上総利益率：60.6%→59.5%
・販管費：60.8億円→82.7億円

売上総利益率は比較的維持されており、装置売上の減少と販管費増加が営業減益の主要因。

一方、装置の生産実績は大きく伸びている。

製造が進む一方、売上計上との間に時間差が生じている可能性も考えられます。ただし、詳細な要因は決算短信だけでは判断できません。

■ AI半導体需要は？

会社側はCPU、GPU、HBMなどの需要が高水準で推移し、半導体メーカーの設備投資計画はさらに積極化したと説明。

さらに、今期の受注見通しは従来想定を上回るとしています。

直近のTSMC、ASML、SKハイニクスの発表も、先端半導体需要の強さを裏付けています。

■ 今後の注目点

通期予想は据え置きですが、達成には残り3四半期で平均832億円の売上が必要。

今回の決算からAI需要の減速を示す明確な材料は見当たりません。

ただし、市場予想との乖離は大きく、今後は受注拡大が計画通り売上・利益に転換するか、特に出荷・検収の進捗を確認したいところです。

French quantum company @Alice__Bob estimates that 22,593 qubits could break RSA-2048 in about three days. It is the smallest estimate I have seen that runs in days. But it needs qubits nobody can build yet.  

The paper is serious work. The team laid out Shor's algorithm qubit by qubit on a chip of cat qubits, and the elliptic-curve version, the math behind Bitcoin keys, comes in at about an hour on at most 29,588 qubits.  

The condition is one assumption: no bit-flips during the run. The paper equates that with a bit-flip time of about 100 years per qubit. The best peer-reviewed measurement with quantum control is 22 seconds. 

Alice & Bob's own preliminary results reach 44 minutes, and about four hours on qubits it has not yet shown it can control as fully. Its largest chip with error-correction results has 12 cat qubits.
